pg-easy-01.syntax:
-- General form
--   expr1 || expr2
-- The operator is chosen by the operand types (operator overloading).
-- Postgres defines || for several type families (text, arrays, bytea, jsonb, tsvector...).

-- Example 1: building a label from columns
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM people;

-- Example 2: array operand
SELECT ARRAY[1,2] || 3;   -- appends an element to an array

-- Gotchas / variations
-- * NULL operand: with plain || the whole result is NULL.
--     SELECT 'a' || NULL;          -- yields NULL
--   concat(a, b, ...) skips NULLs; concat_ws(sep, a, b, ...) adds a separator.
-- * Non-text operand: one side may be a non-text type, which is cast to text.
--     SELECT 'n=' || 42;
--   With two untyped literals or two non-text values, add an explicit cast: 42::text.
-- * Precedence: || binds looser than + and -, so wrap mixed expressions in parentheses.
-- * Logical OR is the keyword OR, not a symbol.
-- * Bytea values use || too, joining the byte strings.
pg-easy-01.title: SQL operators on text values

pg-easy-07.syntax:
-- psql meta-commands start with a backslash and are handled by psql itself,
-- not sent to the server as SQL.
--   \q          quit psql (also \quit)
--   \conninfo   show current connection details
--   \set        show or set psql variables
--   \echo text  print text

-- Explicit transaction control is plain SQL sent to the server:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO audit_log(msg) VALUES ('hello');
-- choose one way to end the transaction:
COMMIT;      -- make changes permanent
-- ROLLBACK; -- discard changes

-- Gotchas (as comments):
-- * psql is only a client; the transaction lives on the server
--   and belongs to the connection.
-- * Think about what the server does when a connection
--   closes while a transaction is still open.
-- * Check state with the prompt: %x in PROMPT1 shows
--   '*' when in a transaction block, '!' when failed.
--     \set PROMPT1 '%/%x%R%# '
-- * \set AUTOCOMMIT off makes psql open a transaction
--   implicitly before your first command; you must
--   COMMIT explicitly.
-- * Ctrl-D (end of input) also ends the session, like \q.
pg-easy-07.title: PostgreSQL client sessions and transactions

pg-easy-08.syntax:
-- psql backslash meta-commands are handled by the psql client, not the server.
-- General form:
--   \command [argument]

-- Display-related toggles (no argument flips the current state):
--   \timing [on|off]    client-side timing of statements
--   \pset [option [value]]   set a table output option
--   \a                  toggle aligned / unaligned output
--   \H                  toggle HTML output
--   \x [on|off|auto]    toggle expanded output mode

-- Example session:
--   mydb=> \pset border 2
--   mydb=> \pset null '(null)'
--   mydb=> \pset format aligned

-- Gotchas:
-- * Calling a toggle with no argument flips it; passing on/off sets it explicitly.
-- * \pset with no arguments lists nothing; use \pset OPTION to show one setting.
-- * Settings last only for the current session unless placed in ~/.psqlrc.
-- * \x auto picks the layout per result, based on terminal width.
-- * Meta-commands end at the end of the line; they take no semicolon.
-- * Related: \pset pager, \pset columns, \pset format (aligned, csv, html, wrapped).
-- * Use \? inside psql to list all meta-commands.
pg-easy-08.title: psql interactive terminal behavior

pg-easy-12.syntax:
-- General form:
--   unquoted_identifier   -> case-insensitive name
--   "Quoted Identifier"   -> exact name, case and spaces preserved

-- Example 1: unquoted names
CREATE TABLE Orders (OrderId int, CustomerName text);
SELECT CustomerName FROM ORDERS;      -- same table and column as above

-- Example 2: quoted names
CREATE TABLE "Invoices" ("InvoiceId" int, total numeric);
SELECT "InvoiceId" FROM "Invoices";   -- must match exactly

-- Gotchas / variations:
-- * The rule applies to identifiers (tables, columns, aliases, functions),
--   not to string literals, which use single quotes and keep their case.
-- * Once created with double quotes and mixed case, every later reference
--   must also be quoted with the same case.
-- * Double quotes also allow reserved words and special characters in names.
-- * Inside a quoted identifier, write a literal double quote as "".
-- * Folding is done by the parser at parse time, so the catalogs
--   (pg_class, information_schema) store the folded form.
-- * Common convention: use lowercase snake_case and avoid quoting.
pg-easy-12.title: SQL identifiers and naming rules

docs.title: Schema search path and name lookup

pg-easy-16.syntax:
-- Unqualified names are resolved using the search_path setting.
-- General form:
--   SHOW search_path;
--   SET search_path TO schema_a, schema_b, ...;
--   CREATE TABLE [schema.]table_name (...);

-- Example: inspect the path and see where a new table lands
SHOW search_path;                      -- lists schemas searched, in order
CREATE TABLE inventory (id int);       -- unqualified: created in the FIRST existing
                                       -- schema on the search_path
SELECT schemaname, tablename
FROM pg_tables
WHERE tablename = 'inventory';         -- shows which schema holds it

-- Example: qualify explicitly or change the path
CREATE SCHEMA staging;
CREATE TABLE staging.orders (id int);  -- explicit schema
SET search_path TO staging, public;    -- now unqualified creates go to staging

-- Gotchas:
-- * The default search_path value is "$user", <default schema>.
--   "$user" is skipped if no schema has the current user's name.
-- * System catalogs (pg_catalog) are always searched implicitly,
--   even if not listed in the path.
-- * information_schema is a standard-views schema, not a place for user tables.
-- * Lookups search in order; creation uses only the first existing schema.
-- * ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path / ALTER DATABASE ... SET makes it persistent.
-- * Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary users lack CREATE on the default schema
--   unless granted.
pg-easy-16.title: PostgreSQL schemas and object name resolution

docs.title: Conflict handling clauses in SQL inserts

pg-easy-21.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table (cols...)
VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT [ conflict_target ] conflict_action;

-- conflict_target is one of:
--   ( col [, ...] )                 -- inference by column list
--   ( expr )                        -- index expression
--   ON CONSTRAINT constraint_name   -- name a constraint directly
--   optional WHERE predicate        -- for partial indexes

-- conflict_action is one of:
--   DO NOTHING
--   DO UPDATE SET col = expr [, ...] [WHERE cond]

-- Example 1: target a column list
CREATE TABLE users (email text UNIQUE, name text);
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Ann')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

-- Example 2: update using the proposed row via EXCLUDED
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Anna')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE
  SET name = EXCLUDED.name;

-- Gotchas
-- * For DO UPDATE the conflict target is required.
--   For DO NOTHING it may be omitted (any conflict is skipped).
-- * A column-list target must match an existing unique index or
--   unique/exclusion-compatible constraint, otherwise an error is raised.
-- * Only conflicts on the inferred index are handled by the clause;
--   a violation of a different unique constraint still raises an error.
-- * RETURNING yields only rows actually inserted or updated;
--   skipped rows are not returned.
-- * One command cannot update the same row twice via DO UPDATE.
pg-easy-21.title: Handling insert conflicts in SQL

pg-easy-26.syntax:
-- General form
--   jsonb_expr -> 'key'      -- object field by key
--   jsonb_expr -> int        -- array element by 0-based index (negative counts from end)
--   jsonb_expr ->> 'key'     -- same lookup, result converted to text
--   jsonb_expr #> '{a,b}'    -- path lookup (jsonb);  #>> returns text

-- Example setup: col `doc` is jsonb = {"shop": {"city": "Oslo", "tags": ["a","b"]}}
SELECT doc -> 'shop'              FROM t;  -- lookup one level
SELECT doc -> 'shop' -> 'city'    FROM t;  -- operators chain left to right
SELECT doc -> 'shop' -> 'tags' -> 0 FROM t;  -- array index
SELECT doc #>> '{shop,city}'      FROM t;  -- path form, text result

-- Gotchas
-- * The result type of -> is jsonb (or json for json columns); ->> is text.
-- * Text key on an object, integer on an array; a mismatch yields NULL.
-- * A missing key or index yields NULL, not an error.
-- * Chaining after ->> fails: text has no -> operator.
-- * Comparing to a string: use ->> 'k' = 'x', or -> 'k' = '"x"'::jsonb.
-- * Operator precedence: parenthesize, e.g. (doc -> 'k') IS NULL.
pg-easy-26.title: PostgreSQL JSON data access

pg-easy-27.syntax:
-- General form
--   jsonb_expr  <operator>  key_or_index
-- Operators that extract a single element:
--   ->   extract an object field by key, or an array element by integer index
--   ->>  same lookup, but with a different result type than ->
-- Path variants (take a text[] path):
--   #>   and   #>>

-- Example table: orders(info jsonb)
-- info = '{"customer": {"city": "Oslo"}, "tags": ["a","b"], "qty": 3}'

SELECT info -> 'customer'              FROM orders;  -- lookup by key
SELECT info -> 'tags' -> 0             FROM orders;  -- chain operators; integer = array index
SELECT info #> '{customer,city}'       FROM orders;  -- path lookup

-- Check the result type with pg_typeof():
SELECT pg_typeof(info -> 'qty'), pg_typeof(info ->> 'qty') FROM orders;

-- Gotchas
-- * Missing key or out-of-range index yields SQL NULL for both operators.
-- * A JSON null value is different from SQL NULL when the result stays jsonb.
-- * Operators can be chained, but the left side must be jsonb (or json).
-- * Casting is needed for numeric comparisons on extracted values:
--     WHERE (info ->> 'qty')::int > 2
-- * Use the result type to decide which operator can be chained further.
-- * Negative integer index counts from the end of an array: info -> 'tags' -> -1
pg-easy-27.title: JSON data access in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-29.syntax:
-- General form (variadic, arguments alternate key, value, key, value, ...)
jsonb_build_object(key1, value1, key2, value2, ...)  -- returns jsonb object
jsonb_build_array(value1, value2, ...)               -- returns jsonb array

-- Examples
SELECT jsonb_build_object('name', 'Ada', 'age', 36, 'admin', false);
SELECT jsonb_build_array('x', 2, NULL, true);

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Arguments are taken in pairs; an odd number of arguments raises an error.
-- * Keys are converted to text; a key cannot be NULL.
-- * Each value keeps its SQL type when converted to JSON:
--     numbers become JSON numbers, booleans become JSON booleans,
--     text becomes JSON strings, NULL becomes JSON null.
-- * Values may be of mixed types (the function accepts "any" arguments).
-- * Values can be nested: another jsonb_build_object(...) or an array.
-- * Untyped literals like 'abc' are treated as text.
-- * json_build_object is the json (not jsonb) variant; jsonb sorts keys
--   and removes duplicate keys (last value wins).
-- * Empty call: jsonb_build_object() returns {}.
pg-easy-29.title: JSON construction functions

pg-easy-33.syntax:
-- General form:
-- COALESCE(value1, value2, ..., valueN)
-- Evaluates arguments left to right and yields the first
-- argument that is not NULL. If all are NULL, yields NULL.

-- Example 1: fallback to a literal
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, 'anonymous') FROM users;

-- Example 2: chain of fallbacks
SELECT COALESCE(mobile_phone, home_phone, work_phone, 'none') AS contact
FROM people;

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * Later arguments are only evaluated if needed (short-circuit).
-- * All arguments must resolve to a compatible common type,
--   otherwise Postgres raises a type error.
-- * Only NULL triggers the fallback; empty strings and 0
--   are real values and are returned as-is.
-- * If every argument is NULL the result is NULL, so end the
--   list with a non-null literal when you need a guaranteed value.
-- * Useful in aggregates: COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) for empty groups.
-- * Related: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b.
pg-easy-33.title: Handling missing values in SQL

pg-easy-34.syntax:
-- General form
COALESCE(value1, value2, ..., valueN)

-- Arguments are evaluated left to right; the result is the
-- first argument that is not NULL. If every argument is NULL,
-- the result is NULL.

-- Example 1: fallback for an optional column
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'guest') AS display_name
FROM users;

-- Example 2: replace NULL in an aggregate
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Later arguments are only evaluated if needed (short-circuit),
--   so COALESCE(x, 1/0) will not error when x is not NULL.
-- * All arguments must resolve to a common data type, or Postgres
--   raises a type error.
-- * An empty string '' is NOT NULL, so COALESCE does not skip it.
--   Use COALESCE(NULLIF(col, ''), 'default') to treat '' as missing.
-- * Equivalent to CASE WHEN v1 IS NOT NULL THEN v1 ... END.
-- * COALESCE is standard SQL; NVL / IFNULL are not Postgres functions.
pg-easy-34.title: SQL conditional expressions

pg-easy-38.syntax:
-- Boolean constants (SQL key words):
--   TRUE | FALSE | NULL (unknown)
-- Also accepted as string literals cast to boolean:
--   'true','t','yes','y','on','1'  /  'false','f','no','n','off','0'
--   (leading/trailing whitespace ignored; string input is case-insensitive)

-- Examples
SELECT TRUE AS a, false AS b;
SELECT 'Yes'::boolean;
CREATE TABLE flags (id int, active boolean DEFAULT true);
INSERT INTO flags VALUES (1, 'on'), (2, FALSE);
SELECT * FROM flags WHERE active IS TRUE;

-- Key words and unquoted identifiers: PostgreSQL folds them
-- to a single case when parsing (lower case for identifiers),
-- so SELECT, select, SeLeCt are the same.
-- Quoted identifiers ("Name") ARE case-sensitive.
-- String literal contents are NOT folded, but boolean input
-- parsing of strings ignores case.

-- Gotchas
--   Output is displayed as t / f in psql.
--   Use IS TRUE / IS NOT TRUE / IS UNKNOWN to handle NULL.
--   Numbers other than '1'/'0' strings are not valid boolean strings.
pg-easy-38.title: SQL keywords and literal values

pg-easy-39.syntax:
-- Column constraint:
--   column_name type CHECK (boolean_expression)
-- Table constraint (may reference several columns):
--   [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (boolean_expression)

CREATE TABLE members (
  age      INTEGER CONSTRAINT age_adult CHECK (age >= 18),
  min_qty  INTEGER,
  max_qty  INTEGER,
  CONSTRAINT qty_order CHECK (min_qty <= max_qty)
);

-- Add to an existing table:
ALTER TABLE members
  ADD CONSTRAINT age_cap CHECK (age < 150);

-- Add without scanning existing rows, validate later:
ALTER TABLE members
  ADD CONSTRAINT age_cap2 CHECK (age < 150) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE members VALIDATE CONSTRAINT age_cap2;

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * The expression must evaluate to boolean.
-- * A row is rejected only if the result is FALSE;
--   TRUE and NULL both pass. Add NOT NULL to forbid NULLs.
-- * Violations raise an error (SQLSTATE 23514) and the
--   statement fails.
-- * Only the row's own columns may be used; no subqueries
--   to other tables. Expression should be immutable.
-- * Auto-generated name looks like table_column_check.
-- * Drop with: ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT name;
pg-easy-39.title: Table constraints and data integrity

pg-easy-46.syntax:
-- General form: functions that take no arguments report session state
-- SELECT <function>();   -- some are also usable without parentheses (e.g. current_user)

-- Examples
SELECT current_user;            -- role the session is running as
SELECT session_user;            -- role that opened the session
SELECT current_schema();        -- first existing schema on search_path
SELECT current_schemas(false);  -- array of schemas searched, excluding implicit ones
SELECT inet_server_port();      -- server port of the connection
SELECT version();               -- server version string

-- Gotchas
-- * Return values describe the current session/connection, not server-wide config.
-- * Many return type name (identifier) or text; names are not the same as OIDs.
-- * OIDs are numeric identifiers in system catalogs (e.g. pg_database.oid),
--   and are looked up there rather than returned by most session functions.
-- * Values may differ between sessions, e.g. after SET ROLE or SET search_path.
-- * Settings in postgresql.conf are read with SHOW or current_setting('name').
-- * pg_database lists all databases in the cluster: SELECT datname, oid FROM pg_database;
pg-easy-46.title: PostgreSQL session information functions

pg-easy-48.syntax:
-- General forms (system information functions and settings)
SELECT <function_or_setting>;
SHOW <parameter>;
SELECT current_setting('<parameter>');

-- Examples of related version-inspection tools
SHOW server_version;                    -- version number text only, e.g. 16.3
SELECT current_setting('server_version_num');  -- integer-style version as text
SELECT current_database(), current_user;       -- other session info functions

-- psql client side (not SQL, run at the psql prompt or shell):
--   \conninfo          -- describes the current connection
--   psql --version     -- prints the client program's version (shell)

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * Server-side functions run on the server, so they describe the server,
--   not the psql program you typed into.
-- * Some functions return descriptive text, others return a bare number;
--   check the return type with pg_typeof(...), e.g.
--     SELECT pg_typeof(current_setting('server_version_num'));
-- * current_setting() returns text, so cast it when comparing numerically:
--     SELECT current_setting('server_version_num')::int >= 140000;
-- * Application code should prefer the numeric setting for version checks
--   rather than parsing descriptive text.
-- * Migration tools keep their own schema version tables; Postgres itself
--   has no built-in notion of an application schema version.
pg-easy-48.title: PostgreSQL system information

pg-easy-49.syntax:
-- General form: how a client picks the server endpoint
--   postgresql://user@host:PORT/dbname
--   psql -h HOST -p PORT -U USER -d DBNAME

-- Server side (postgresql.conf):
--   port = <integer>              -- TCP port the server listens on
--   listen_addresses = 'localhost' -- which interfaces to bind
--   unix_socket_directories = '/var/run/postgresql'

-- Example: connecting to a server configured for a custom port
--   psql -h db.example.com -p 6543 -U app -d shop
--   postgresql://app@db.example.com:6543/shop

-- Inspect the running server's setting from SQL:
SHOW port;
SELECT name, setting, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'port';

-- Gotchas:
-- * If -p / the URL port / PGPORT is omitted, the client uses its compiled-in
--   default (the same default the server ships with).
-- * Changing port requires a server restart, not just a reload.
-- * The port also names the Unix socket file (.s.PGSQL.<port>).
-- * Several clusters on one host each need a distinct port.
-- * Other database products use their own, different default ports;
--   do not assume one product's port applies to another.
-- * Env var PGPORT sets the client's default port.
pg-easy-49.title: Database server networking basics

pg-easy-57.syntax:
-- General form:
-- regexp_replace(source, pattern, replacement [, flags])
-- regexp_replace(source, pattern, replacement, start [, N [, flags]])  -- PG 15+

-- Examples (different inputs):
SELECT regexp_replace('a.b.c.d', '\.', ':');        -- one replacement, see flags below
SELECT regexp_replace('a.b.c.d', '\.', ':', 'g');   -- flag changes scope
SELECT regexp_replace('Hello World', 'o', '0', 'gi');
SELECT regexp_replace('John Smith', '(\w+) (\w+)', '\2, \1');  -- backrefs \1..\9

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * Pattern is a POSIX regular expression, not a literal string.
-- * Without flags, only the FIRST match is replaced.
-- * 'g' = replace all matches (global); 'i' = case-insensitive;
--   flags can be combined, e.g. 'gi'.
-- * Replacement: \1-\9 insert captured groups, \& inserts whole match;
--   write \\ for a literal backslash.
-- * If there is no match, the source string is returned unchanged.
-- * Result is text. Input is not modified.
-- * For plain literal replacement of all occurrences, replace(src, from, to)
--   is simpler and does not use regex.
-- * Invalid regex or unknown flag raises an error.
pg-easy-57.title: Text pattern handling in SQL

docs.title: SQL commands for bulk data transfer

pg-easy-64.syntax:
-- Server-side form (SQL command):
COPY table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)];
COPY table_name | (query) TO 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)];

-- Client-side form (psql meta-command, one line, no trailing semicolon needed):
\copy table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)]
\copy (query) TO 'path' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)]

-- Examples:
COPY invoices TO '/var/lib/postgresql/out/invoices.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);
\copy invoices FROM 'invoices_in.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * COPY with a file name: the file is read/written by the server process,
--   path resolved on the server's filesystem, using the server OS account's permissions.
-- * COPY with a file needs superuser or membership in pg_read_server_files /
--   pg_write_server_files; PROGRAM needs pg_execute_server_program.
-- * \copy: psql opens the file itself as the client user, then streams the data
--   to the server via COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT. Path is relative to psql's
--   working directory.
-- * COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT transfers data over the connection (used by drivers).
-- * Options: FORMAT text|csv|binary, DELIMITER, NULL, HEADER, QUOTE, ESCAPE.
-- * COPY is not a normal INSERT: it is fast, and triggers fire but rules do not.
-- * Whole load fails if any row is bad (unless ON_ERROR is set in newer versions).
pg-easy-64.title: Bulk data import and export in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-67.syntax:
-- General forms
nextval(regclass)  -> bigint
currval(regclass)  -> bigint
lastval()          -> bigint
setval(regclass, bigint [, is_called boolean]) -> bigint

-- Example setup
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no START 100 INCREMENT 5;

SELECT currval('order_no');      -- error if nextval not yet called in this session
SELECT setval('order_no', 500);  -- next nextval returns 505
SELECT setval('order_no', 500, false); -- next nextval returns 500
SELECT lastval();                -- latest value returned by nextval in this session, any sequence

-- Typical use
INSERT INTO orders(id, item) VALUES (nextval('order_no'), 'pen');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence state is shared by all sessions; currval/lastval are session-local.
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are not rolled back
--   on ROLLBACK, so gaps in values are normal.
-- * Concurrent sessions each receive distinct values, never blocked by
--   other transactions' uncommitted calls.
-- * CACHE n makes a session preallocate values; other sessions may see
--   out-of-order values.
-- * Argument is regclass: a quoted name, resolved via search_path;
--   use 'schema.seq' to be explicit.
-- * serial / identity columns use a sequence behind the scenes.
pg-easy-67.title: PostgreSQL sequences

pg-easy-68.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_name [INCREMENT BY n] [START WITH n] [CACHE n] [CYCLE];
SELECT nextval('seq_name');   -- advance and return the new value
SELECT currval('seq_name');  -- last value nextval returned in THIS session
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100);         -- set current value explicitly
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100, false);  -- next nextval returns 100

-- Example
CREATE SEQUENCE invoice_no START 500;
CREATE TABLE invoice (id bigint DEFAULT nextval('invoice_no'), note text);
INSERT INTO invoice (note) VALUES ('first');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are designed so that
--   concurrent sessions never block each other on nextval.
-- * Consider how the effect of nextval interacts with transaction
--   commit/abort, and what that means for numbering continuity.
-- * Other causes of unused numbers: failed INSERTs, CACHE preallocation,
--   crash recovery.
-- * currval errors if nextval was not yet called in the session.
-- * serial / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY columns use sequences internally,
--   so they follow the same rules.
-- * Do not rely on sequences for gap-free numbering; use a separate
--   counter table with row locking if that is required.
pg-easy-68.title: Database sequences and transactions

pg-easy-70.syntax:
-- General form
-- column_name data_type [ DEFAULT default_expr ] [ constraints ]
-- default_expr is a value expression evaluated per row at INSERT time
-- whenever the column is not supplied (omitted or DEFAULT keyword).

CREATE TABLE ticket (
  id        BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  status    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  priority  INT DEFAULT 3,
  opened_on DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- Default applies: column omitted, or DEFAULT keyword used
INSERT INTO ticket (priority) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO ticket (status, priority) VALUES (DEFAULT, 2);

-- Change or remove a default later (affects only future inserts)
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority SET DEFAULT 5;
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority DROP DEFAULT;

-- Gotchas
-- * An explicit NULL is stored as NULL; the default is NOT used.
-- * A default does not imply NOT NULL; add that constraint separately.
-- * A default is not applied by UPDATE (use a trigger for that).
-- * Volatile functions (random(), clock_timestamp()) run per row;
--   now() returns the current transaction's start time.
-- * Defaults cannot reference other columns or contain subqueries.
-- * Without DEFAULT, an omitted column becomes NULL.
pg-easy-70.title: Column defaults in table definitions

pg-easy-71.syntax:
-- General form: a function call returning a value of type uuid
--   <function_name>()

-- Example: using a UUID generator as a column default
CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id    uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT <uuid_function>(),
    label text
);

INSERT INTO invoices (label) VALUES ('march') RETURNING id;

-- Call it directly in a query:
SELECT <uuid_function>();

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * The result has type uuid (128-bit), shown as 8-4-4-4-12 hex digits.
-- * Core Postgres (13+) provides gen_random_uuid() with no extension needed;
--   older versions needed the pgcrypto extension.
-- * Newer versions (18+) also add uuidv4() and uuidv7(); check the docs
--   for what each version-specific function guarantees.
-- * The uuid-ossp extension offers other generators, e.g. uuid_generate_v1(),
--   uuid_generate_v3()/v5() (namespace + name based).
-- * Each call is evaluated per row when used in DEFAULT or SELECT lists.
-- * The ordering of generated values affects index locality on a primary key.
pg-easy-71.title: UUID generation in PostgreSQL

docs.title: psql meta-commands for inspecting database objects

pg-easy-73.syntax:
-- General form (run inside psql, not as SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S+] [pattern]
-- The letter after \d picks the kind of object to list.
-- Suffix + adds more detail (size, description, etc.).
-- Suffix S includes system objects.
-- pattern is an optional name filter; supports * and ?.

-- Examples:
--   \dv+ report_*     -- views whose names start with report_, with detail
--   \dT               -- user-defined data types

-- Common letters in the family:
--   \d name   describe one relation (columns, indexes)
--   \dt       tables
--   \dv       views
--   \di       indexes
--   \ds       sequences
--   \dn       schemas
--   \df       functions
--   \du       roles
--   \dT       data types
--   \dE       foreign tables
--   \l        databases (not a \d form)

-- Gotchas:
--   * Letters are case-sensitive: \dt and \dT differ.
--   * Meta-commands are psql features, not server SQL;
--     they work by querying the system catalogs.
--   * Use psql -E to echo the SQL a meta-command runs.
--   * Another letter in this family covers installed
--     extensions; check \? for the full list.
--   * Without a pattern, only objects visible on the
--     search_path are listed for many kinds.
pg-easy-73.title: psql meta-commands

pg-easy-81.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not sent to the server):
--   \meta-command [arguments]

-- Commands that take a file name:
\i  filename        -- \include
\ir filename        -- \include_relative (path relative to the current script)
\copy table FROM 'file' ...   -- client-side bulk data load/export
\o  filename        -- send query output to a file
\e  [filename]      -- open an editor

-- Examples with other names:
\i  /tmp/migrations/001_schema.sql
\ir ../seed/data.sql

-- Related, from the shell rather than inside psql:
--   psql -f file.sql dbname      (run a file, then exit)
--   psql -c 'SELECT 1' dbname    (run one command string)

-- Notes and gotchas:
-- * Backslash commands are handled by psql itself, not by the server.
-- * Relative paths in \i resolve against psql's current working directory;
--   use \ir inside nested scripts to resolve against the calling script.
-- * Errors in a file do not stop it by default; set ON_ERROR_STOP to on to abort.
-- * Files are read on the client machine, not the server.
-- * \copy moves data rows; it does not execute SQL statements found in a file.
-- * Use \? to list all meta-commands and \? variables for settings.
pg-easy-81.title: PostgreSQL interactive terminal basics

docs.title: PostgreSQL conditional expressions and related functions

pg-easy-85.syntax:
-- General form
GREATEST(value [, ...])
LEAST(value [, ...])

-- Examples
SELECT LEAST(10, 4, 8);            -- picks from the list of arguments
SELECT GREATEST('apple', 'pear');  -- works on text using collation ordering
SELECT GREATEST(price, 0) FROM items;  -- per-row clamp to a floor

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Takes one or more expressions; returns a single scalar value, not an array.
-- * All arguments must resolve to a common data type (same rules as UNION/CASE);
--   mixing int and numeric promotes to numeric.
-- * NULL arguments are ignored; the result is NULL only if ALL arguments are NULL.
--   (This differs from the MAX()/MIN() aggregates' behavior across rows? No: those
--   also skip NULLs, but they work over rows, not over an argument list.)
-- * GREATEST/LEAST compare values within one row; MAX/MIN aggregate across rows.
-- * To compare values from an array, use an aggregate or unnest:
--     SELECT max(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[5,9,1]) AS x;
pg-easy-85.title: SQL conditional expressions

pg-easy-87.syntax:
-- General forms
--   to_char(value, 'pattern')       -> text
--   to_date(text, 'pattern')        -> ?
--   to_timestamp(text, 'pattern')   -> ?
--   to_number(text, 'pattern')      -> numeric

-- Examples (different values)
SELECT to_char(now(), 'DD Mon YYYY');
SELECT to_date('15/08/2023', 'DD/MM/YYYY');
SELECT to_timestamp('2023-08-15 14:30', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI');

-- Common pattern tokens
--   YYYY year, MM month number, Mon abbreviated month name,
--   DD day of month, HH24 hour 0-23, MI minute, SS second

-- Gotchas
-- * The pattern describes how the input text is laid out; it is not validated
--   like a strict parser: extra or mismatched separators are often tolerated.
-- * Fields missing from the input take defaults (e.g. no day -> day 1).
-- * Out-of-range values raise an error (e.g. month 13), not NULL.
-- * No built-in boolean 'is valid date' function; wrap a cast in
--   exception handling (PL/pgSQL) or validate with a regex.
-- * For ISO-style text, a plain cast works: '2023-08-15'::date
-- * Check each function's return type in the docs before relying on it.
pg-easy-87.title: Date and time conversion functions

pg-easy-94.title: PostgreSQL runtime configuration settings

pg-easy-02.syntax:
-- General form: string concatenation
-- text || text            -> text
-- text || anynonarray      -> text (non-string operand is cast to text)
-- concat(val1, val2, ...)  -> text
-- concat_ws(sep, val1, ...) -> text

SELECT 'Post' || 'greSQL';          -- 'PostgreSQL'
SELECT 'Value: ' || 42;             -- 'Value: 42'

-- Gotcha: || is a strict operator. If either operand is NULL,
-- the whole result is NULL.
SELECT 'x' || NULL::text;           -- NULL
SELECT first_name || ' ' || middle_name FROM people;  -- NULL whenever middle_name IS NULL

-- Workarounds:
SELECT 'x' || coalesce(NULL, '');   -- 'x'
SELECT concat('x', NULL, 'y');      -- 'xy'  (concat ignores NULL arguments)
SELECT concat_ws('-', 'a', NULL, 'b'); -- 'a-b' (NULLs skipped, separator not doubled)

-- Note: concat_ws returns NULL only if the separator itself is NULL.
-- Note: an empty string '' is NOT NULL in Postgres (unlike Oracle).
-- Note: 'a' || NULL with untyped NULL resolves to text || text -> NULL.
pg-easy-02.title: String functions and operators

pg-easy-03.syntax:
-- General form
-- string LIKE pattern [ESCAPE escape_char]
-- string ILIKE pattern [ESCAPE escape_char]
-- string NOT LIKE / NOT ILIKE pattern
-- Wildcards: % = any sequence of chars, _ = exactly one char

-- Case-sensitive: matches 'Paris' but not 'paris'
SELECT city FROM offices WHERE city LIKE 'Par%';

-- Case-insensitive: matches 'Paris', 'PARIS', 'paris'
SELECT city FROM offices WHERE city ILIKE 'par%';

-- Operator shorthands:
--   ~~  = LIKE      ~~*  = ILIKE
--   !~~ = NOT LIKE  !~~* = NOT ILIKE
SELECT 'Berlin' ~~* 'ber%';  -- true

-- Gotchas:
-- ILIKE is a PostgreSQL extension, not standard SQL;
--   portable alternative: lower(col) LIKE lower('...')
-- Pattern must match the WHOLE string; use % at both ends
--   for 'contains': col ILIKE '%lon%'
-- Default escape char is backslash: '50\%' matches literal '50%'
-- Both use the same % and _ wildcards; for regex use ~ or ~*
-- Neither is limited to one line; % also matches newlines
-- A plain B-tree index can help left-anchored LIKE only with
--   C collation or text_pattern_ops; ILIKE usually needs a
--   pg_trgm GIN/GiST index or an index on lower(col)
pg-easy-03.title: Pattern matching

pg-easy-05.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not SQL; no semicolon needed)
-- \command [pattern]      add + for extra detail, S to include system objects

-- List all databases on the server
\l
\l+            -- also shows size, tablespace, description
\l sales*      -- only databases whose names match the pattern

-- Other common listing commands
\dt            -- tables in the current search_path
\dt inventory.* -- tables in schema inventory
\dn            -- schemas
\du            -- roles (users/groups)
\di            -- indexes
\dv            -- views
\df            -- functions
\d orders      -- describe one relation (columns, indexes)

-- Switch to another database
\c analytics

-- Gotchas:
-- \l lists databases cluster-wide; \dt and friends only see the current database.
-- \list is the long form of \l.
-- From the shell: psql -l lists databases without opening a session.
-- Patterns use * and ? wildcards, not SQL LIKE's % and _.
-- \? shows help for all meta-commands; \h shows help for SQL commands.
pg-easy-05.title: psql meta-commands

pg-easy-10.syntax:
-- General form: serial pseudo-types create an integer column
-- plus an owned sequence and a DEFAULT nextval(...)
CREATE TABLE t (col SMALLSERIAL | SERIAL | BIGSERIAL);

-- Example
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- bigint, 1 .. 9223372036854775807
  line_no   SERIAL                  -- integer, 1 .. 2147483647
);

-- Roughly equivalent to:
-- CREATE SEQUENCE orders_line_no_seq AS integer;
-- line_no integer NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval('orders_line_no_seq')
-- ALTER SEQUENCE orders_line_no_seq OWNED BY orders.line_no;

-- Ranges / storage:
-- SMALLSERIAL = smallint, 2 bytes, 1 .. 32767
-- SERIAL      = integer,  4 bytes, 1 .. 2147483647
-- BIGSERIAL   = bigint,   8 bytes, 1 .. 9223372036854775807

-- Gotchas:
-- * Not true types: no UNIQUE/PK added automatically.
-- * Gaps occur (rolled-back txns consume values).
-- * SERIAL can run out on busy tables; prefer BIGSERIAL.
-- * Modern alternative: col bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
pg-easy-10.title: Numeric data types

pg-easy-14.syntax:
-- General form
-- column_name TEXT              -- unlimited length
-- column_name VARCHAR(n)        -- length limit n characters (checked on write)
-- column_name CHAR(n)           -- blank-padded to n characters

CREATE TABLE customer (
  id      bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  nick    text,                          -- no limit
  country varchar(2),                    -- errors if longer than 2
  sku     text CHECK (char_length(sku) <= 12)  -- limit via constraint
);

INSERT INTO customer VALUES (1, 'zed', 'NZ', 'AB-1001');
-- INSERT ... country = 'NZL'  -> ERROR: value too long for type character varying(2)

-- Performance: text, varchar(n) and varchar share the same varlena storage.
-- There is no speed or size advantage to varchar(n); the length check adds
-- a tiny cost on write. char(n) is usually the slowest (padding).
-- Short values (< 127 bytes) use a 1-byte header; long ones may be TOASTed.
-- Gotchas:
--   varchar without (n) behaves like text.
--   Explicit cast 'abcdef'::varchar(3) silently truncates to 'abc'.
--   Raising a varchar(n) limit later needs ALTER TABLE; a CHECK is easier to change.
--   char(n) trailing spaces are ignored in comparisons.
pg-easy-14.title: Character data types

pg-easy-15.syntax:
-- General form
-- character(n) / char(n)              fixed length, blank-padded
-- character varying(n) / varchar(n)   variable length, limit n
-- text                                 variable, unlimited

CREATE TABLE codes (
  tag   char(6),
  label varchar(20),
  note  text
);

INSERT INTO codes VALUES ('ab', 'ab', 'ab');

SELECT octet_length(tag),   -- 6: stored as 'ab' + 4 trailing spaces
       length(tag),         -- 2: trailing spaces ignored for char(n)
       octet_length(label)  -- 2: varchar is not padded
FROM codes;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Shorter values in char(n) are padded with trailing spaces to n.
-- * Longer values raise an error unless the excess is all spaces
--   (then it is truncated silently).
-- * Explicit cast 'abcdefgh'::char(3) truncates to 'abc', no error.
-- * char(n) trailing spaces are insignificant in comparisons:
--   'ab'::char(4) = 'ab  '::char(4) is true.
-- * Casting char(n) to text/varchar drops trailing spaces.
-- * char without (n) means char(1).
-- * No performance benefit for char(n); text or varchar is preferred.
pg-easy-15.title: Character data types

pg-easy-20.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2, ...)
VALUES (...)
[ ON CONFLICT [ conflict_target ] conflict_action ]
[ RETURNING ... ];

-- conflict_target: (col, ...) | ON CONSTRAINT constraint_name
-- conflict_action: DO NOTHING
--                | DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col [WHERE ...]

-- Skip rows that would violate a unique constraint
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@example.com')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;   -- reports INSERT 0 0, no error

-- Upsert: update the existing row instead
INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('X9', 5)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;

-- Gotchas:
-- * DO NOTHING may omit the conflict target; DO UPDATE requires one.
-- * Other rows in a multi-row INSERT are still inserted; nothing is
--   rolled back, and the transaction stays healthy.
-- * Only unique/exclusion constraint conflicts are handled; NOT NULL,
--   CHECK, and foreign-key violations still raise errors.
-- * RETURNING yields no row for skipped inserts.
-- * EXCLUDED refers to the row proposed for insertion.
-- * DO UPDATE cannot touch the same row twice in one statement.
pg-easy-20.title: Inserting data

pg-easy-22.syntax:
-- General form: array constructor
ARRAY[expr1, expr2, ...]
-- Alternative: string literal cast to an array type
'{val1,val2,...}'::type[]

-- Examples
SELECT ARRAY[10, 20, 30];            -- {10,20,30} (integer[])
SELECT ARRAY['red', 'green'];        -- {red,green} (text[])
SELECT '{4,5,6}'::int[];             -- {4,5,6}
SELECT ARRAY[[1,2],[3,4]];           -- 2-D array {{1,2},{3,4}}

-- Variations & gotchas
-- Square brackets, not parentheses: ARRAY(...) is a different form that
--   takes a subquery, e.g. ARRAY(SELECT id FROM users ORDER BY id)
-- Text literal form uses curly braces '{...}', not '[...]'
-- Empty array needs an explicit type: ARRAY[]::text[]  or  '{}'::text[]
-- Element types must be compatible; cast if needed: ARRAY[1, 2.5]::numeric[]
-- Arrays are 1-based: (ARRAY[7,8,9])[1] -> 7
-- Slices: (ARRAY[7,8,9])[2:3] -> {8,9}
-- Membership: 8 = ANY(ARRAY[7,8,9]) -> true
pg-easy-22.title: Array types

pg-easy-23.syntax:
-- Array literal (text form), cast to an array type
'{elem1,elem2,...}'::type[]
-- Array constructor syntax
ARRAY[expr1, expr2, ...]

-- Examples
SELECT '{10,20,30}'::int[];          -- {10,20,30}
SELECT ARRAY[10,20,30];              -- {10,20,30}
SELECT '{a,b}'::text[] = ARRAY['a','b'];  -- true

-- Multidimensional
SELECT '{{1,2},{3,4}}'::int[];
SELECT ARRAY[[1,2],[3,4]];

-- Gotchas:
-- * Literal form: elements are parsed as text by the element type's
--   input function; quote elements containing commas, braces, spaces:
--   '{"x,y","z"}'::text[]
-- * NULL (unquoted) in a literal is a null element; "NULL" is a string.
-- * ARRAY[...] elements are SQL expressions; type is inferred from
--   them. Empty needs a cast: ARRAY[]::int[]  or  '{}'::int[]
-- * Arrays are 1-based by default: (ARRAY[5,6,7])[1] -> 5
-- * Custom bounds via literal: '[0:1]={8,9}'::int[]
-- * Delimiter is ',' for most types (box uses ';').
pg-easy-23.title: Array types

pg-easy-24.syntax:
-- General form: subscript an array value
-- array_expr[index]          -- single element
-- array_expr[lower:upper]    -- slice (returns an array)

SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d'])[2];    -- 'b'
SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d'])[2:3];  -- {b,c}

-- Column references need no parentheses
SELECT tags[1] FROM posts;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Default lower bound is 1, not 0; [0] is valid syntax but
--   usually returns NULL.
-- * Out-of-range subscripts return NULL, not an error.
-- * Wrap a constructor or function result in parentheses before
--   subscripting: (ARRAY[...])[n], (string_to_array(s, ','))[1].
--   Only a plain column reference or positional parameter
--   may omit them.
-- * Omitted slice bounds: arr[:2], arr[3:]
-- * Multi-dim: matrix[row][col]
-- * array_lower(arr, 1) and array_upper(arr, 1) report the bounds;
--   cardinality(arr) gives the total element count.
pg-easy-24.title: Array types and expressions

pg-easy-28.syntax:
-- General form: does the left jsonb contain the right jsonb?
-- jsonb_left @> jsonb_right   -> boolean
-- jsonb_left <@ jsonb_right   -> boolean (is left contained in right?)

SELECT '{"name": "kim", "role": "admin", "age": 40}'::jsonb
       @> '{"role": "admin"}'::jsonb;          -- true

SELECT '{"tags": ["red", "blue", "green"]}'::jsonb
       @> '{"tags": ["green"]}'::jsonb;        -- true (nested array subset)

-- Values must match, not just keys:
SELECT '{"role": "admin"}'::jsonb @> '{"role": "user"}'::jsonb;  -- false

-- Arrays: order and duplicates are ignored
SELECT '[3, 1, 2]'::jsonb @> '[1, 1, 3]'::jsonb;   -- true

-- Gotchas:
-- * Matching is recursive/structural: nested objects must match too.
-- * A primitive in an array: '["x", 5]' @> '"x"' is true (special case).
-- * Key-only checks use ? , ?| , ?& instead.
-- * Only for jsonb, not plain json.
-- * GIN indexes (jsonb_ops or jsonb_path_ops) speed up @> queries:
--   CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (body jsonb_path_ops);
pg-easy-28.title: JSON operators

pg-easy-30.syntax:
-- Current date/time functions (no parentheses for SQL-standard forms)
-- now() / CURRENT_TIMESTAMP / transaction_timestamp() -> start of current TRANSACTION
-- statement_timestamp()  -> start of current statement
-- clock_timestamp()      -> actual wall-clock time, changes during a statement
-- CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME, LOCALTIME, LOCALTIMESTAMP -> also transaction start

BEGIN;
SELECT transaction_timestamp();   -- e.g. 2024-03-05 09:00:00.12+00
SELECT pg_sleep(3);
SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;         -- same value as above (frozen per transaction)
SELECT clock_timestamp();         -- ~3 seconds later
COMMIT;

-- clock_timestamp() differs even within one statement:
SELECT clock_timestamp(), clock_timestamp();  -- two different values

-- Gotchas:
-- * Outside an explicit BEGIN, each statement is its own transaction,
--   so now() changes between separate statements.
-- * Use clock_timestamp() to measure elapsed time inside a transaction.
-- * CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(2) / LOCALTIMESTAMP(0) accept a precision argument.
-- * 'now'::timestamp is evaluated at parse time; avoid it in DEFAULT clauses.
pg-easy-30.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-31.syntax:
-- General form: current date/time values (fixed at transaction start)
SELECT CURRENT_DATE;                -- type: date
SELECT CURRENT_TIME;                -- type: time with time zone
SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;           -- type: timestamp with time zone
SELECT now();                       -- same as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (timestamptz)
SELECT LOCALTIME, LOCALTIMESTAMP;   -- time / timestamp WITHOUT time zone

-- Examples
SELECT order_id FROM shipments
WHERE  shipped_on = CURRENT_DATE - 1;          -- date - integer = date

SELECT pg_typeof(CURRENT_DATE), pg_typeof(now());
-- date | timestamp with time zone

-- Variations & gotchas:
-- * CURRENT_DATE/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP take no parentheses; now() needs them.
-- * CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(2) / LOCALTIMESTAMP(0) set fractional-second precision.
-- * All of these return the transaction START time, constant within a txn.
--   Use clock_timestamp() for the real wall-clock time, statement_timestamp()
--   for the statement start.
-- * now()::date and CURRENT_DATE both depend on the session TimeZone setting.
-- * date_trunc('day', now()) stays timestamptz (midnight), not a date.
-- * 'now'::timestamptz in a DEFAULT is evaluated once at table creation; use now().
pg-easy-31.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-32.syntax:
-- General form: current date/time functions
-- Transaction-start time (fixed for the whole transaction):
--   now(), current_timestamp, transaction_timestamp()
-- Statement-start time:
--   statement_timestamp()
-- Actual wall-clock time (changes during a statement):
--   clock_timestamp(), timeofday()  -- timeofday() returns text

BEGIN;
SELECT transaction_timestamp() AS tx_start,
       statement_timestamp()   AS stmt_start,
       clock_timestamp()       AS wall_clock;
SELECT pg_sleep(1.5);
SELECT now() AS still_tx_start,     -- same as before
       clock_timestamp() AS later;  -- about 1.5s later
COMMIT;

-- Measure elapsed time inside one statement:
SELECT clock_timestamp() - statement_timestamp() AS elapsed;

-- Gotchas:
-- * now() = current_timestamp = transaction_timestamp().
-- * current_timestamp is written with no parentheses; current_timestamp(3)
--   sets the precision.
-- * clock_timestamp() is VOLATILE, so it can differ between rows of the same
--   query (for example, generate_series rows).
-- * In a DEFAULT, now() gives every row inserted in the transaction the same value.
-- * localtimestamp and localtime return values without a time zone.
pg-easy-32.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-36.syntax:
-- General form
SELECT DISTINCT ON (expr1 [, expr2 ...]) col_list
FROM tbl
ORDER BY expr1 [, expr2 ...], tiebreak_expr [ASC|DESC];

-- Latest reading per sensor
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sensor_id) sensor_id, reading, taken_at
FROM readings
ORDER BY sensor_id, taken_at DESC;

-- Cheapest product per category (id breaks ties)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY category, price, id;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Keeps the FIRST row of each group of rows equal on the
--   DISTINCT ON expressions. "First" is unpredictable unless
--   ORDER BY sorts so the wanted row comes first.
-- * The leftmost ORDER BY items must match the DISTINCT ON
--   expressions (an error is raised otherwise).
-- * Add extra ORDER BY columns after them to choose the row;
--   add a unique column (e.g. id) to break remaining ties.
-- * With no ORDER BY at all, the row kept per group can vary
--   between runs or plans: it is not deterministic.
-- * Plain DISTINCT removes rows that are duplicates across
--   all selected columns, which is a different operation.
pg-easy-36.title: Query result deduplication

pg-easy-37.syntax:
-- General form: boolean column accepts TRUE, FALSE, NULL
-- plus certain quoted string literals (unknown-type input)
CREATE TABLE flags (id int, active boolean);

-- Keyword literals (preferred, SQL standard)
INSERT INTO flags VALUES (10, TRUE), (11, FALSE), (12, NULL);

-- Quoted string input forms (case-insensitive, leading/trailing space ok)
-- true:  'true' 't' 'yes' 'y' 'on' '1'
-- false: 'false' 'f' 'no' 'n' 'off' '0'
INSERT INTO flags VALUES (13, 'on'), (14, 'n');

-- Unique prefixes also work: 'tr', 'fa', 'ye'
-- But 'o' is ambiguous (on/off) -> error

-- Gotchas:
-- Bare integers are NOT accepted: int -> boolean cast is explicit only
--   INSERT INTO flags VALUES (15, 0);       -- ERROR
--   INSERT INTO flags VALUES (15, 0::boolean); -- ok
-- Quoted '0'/'1' are fine (string input, not integer)
-- Empty string '' is not NULL and not valid boolean input -> error
-- Unrecognized words (e.g. 'perhaps') -> invalid input syntax error
-- Output is always displayed as t / f in psql
-- Use IS TRUE / IS NOT FALSE to handle NULLs explicitly
pg-easy-37.title: Data types

pg-easy-42.syntax:
-- General form: list tables via the Postgres catalog view
SELECT schemaname, tablename, tableowner, tablespace,
       hasindexes, hasrules, hastriggers, rowsecurity
FROM pg_catalog.pg_tables
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema');

-- Example: tables with row-level security enabled
SELECT schemaname, tablename
FROM pg_tables
WHERE rowsecurity;

-- Example: the portable SQL-standard alternative
SELECT table_schema, table_name, table_type
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'inventory';

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- pg_tables is Postgres-specific: exposes tablespace, owner,
--   index/rule/trigger flags and rowsecurity.
-- information_schema is SQL-standard (portable) but omits
--   Postgres-only details; it also lists views (table_type = 'VIEW').
-- Both only cover the CURRENT database; catalogs are per-database.
-- Neither gives row counts or sizes: use pg_class.reltuples,
--   pg_stat_user_tables.n_live_tup, or pg_total_relation_size().
-- information_schema shows only objects you have privileges on;
--   pg_tables lists all tables regardless.
-- tablespace is NULL when the table uses the database default.
pg-easy-42.title: System catalogs and metadata

pg-easy-45.syntax:
-- General form (psql client command, not SQL; no semicolon needed)
\timing [ on | off ]

-- Example: toggle on, then run a query
\timing on
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
--  count
-- -------
--   4821
-- (1 row)
--
-- Time: 3.142 ms

\timing off   -- explicitly disable
\timing       -- no argument: toggles current state

-- Gotchas:
-- * Measured by the client: includes network round-trip and
--   result transfer, not just server execution time.
-- * Output is in milliseconds; long runs also show e.g. 01:02.345.
-- * Applies to every subsequent statement until turned off.
-- * For server-side timing per plan node, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
-- * Put \timing on in ~/.psqlrc to enable it by default.
pg-easy-45.title: psql meta-commands

pg-easy-47.syntax:
-- General form: no parentheses (SQL-standard keywords)
SELECT current_user, session_user, current_role;

-- current_user  = role whose privileges are used for permission checks right now
-- session_user  = role that authenticated (the login role)
-- current_role  = same as current_user
-- user          = same as current_user

-- Example: switch identity inside a session
SET ROLE report_reader;
SELECT current_user, session_user;
--  current_user  | session_user
--  report_reader | app_login

RESET ROLE;   -- back to session_user's identity

-- Inside a SECURITY DEFINER function, current_user is the function owner
CREATE FUNCTION whoami() RETURNS name
  LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER
  AS 'SELECT current_user';

-- Gotchas:
-- * Write current_user, not current_user(): the parenthesized form is a syntax error.
-- * SET ROLE changes current_user but never session_user.
-- * SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION (superuser only) changes both.
-- * Database owner and OS user are unrelated:
--   use pg_database.datdba for the owner.
-- * Compare with a role name: WHERE owner = current_user
pg-easy-47.title: Session information functions

pg-easy-50.syntax:
-- General form: two equivalent ways to convert a value to another type
-- expression::target_type          (PostgreSQL-specific shorthand)
-- CAST(expression AS target_type)  (SQL-standard form)

SELECT '2024-03-15'::date;          -- text literal -> date
SELECT CAST('2024-03-15' AS date);  -- same result

SELECT 7::numeric / 2;              -- 3.5000000000000000 (not integer division)
SELECT price::text || ' USD' FROM products;

-- Gotchas:
-- :: binds tighter than most operators: -5::int is -(5::int).
--   Use parentheses: (a + b)::bigint
-- Invalid input raises an error, e.g. 'abc'::integer
--   -> invalid input syntax for type integer
-- Converting to a narrower type can round or truncate:
--   3.7::int = 4, 'hello'::varchar(3) = 'hel'
-- Alternative function-like form for some types: int8('42'), date('2024-01-01')
-- typename 'literal' form works for literals only: DATE '2024-03-15'
-- Not schema qualification: schema.table uses a dot
-- Not a column alias: use AS name for that
-- Arrays: '{1,2,3}'::int[]
pg-easy-50.title: SQL expression syntax

pg-easy-51.syntax:
-- General forms of a type cast
CAST ( expression AS type )   -- SQL-standard syntax
expression::type              -- historical PostgreSQL syntax
type 'string literal'         -- typed literal (string constants only)
typename ( expression )       -- function-like syntax (only some type names)

-- Examples
SELECT CAST('2024-03-15' AS date);       -- 2024-03-15
SELECT '42.7'::numeric(5,1);             -- 42.7
SELECT date '2024-03-15';                -- typed literal
SELECT float8(7);                        -- function-like cast

-- Variations and gotchas
-- CAST(x AS t) and x::t are equivalent: both invoke the same
--   conversion and give the same result.
-- :: binds tighter than most operators, so add parentheses:
--   SELECT -5::text;        -- unary minus applied after ::text, fails
--   SELECT (-5)::text;      -- '-5'
--   SELECT (2 + 3)::text;   -- '5'
-- Casting a value that is not valid for the type raises an error:
--   SELECT 'abc'::int;      -- ERROR: invalid input syntax
-- Casts can be chained: SELECT '3.9'::numeric::int;  -- 4 (rounds)
-- Casting to a length-limited type such as varchar(n) truncates
--   silently with an explicit cast; an implicit assignment raises an error.
-- \dC in psql lists the casts that are defined.
pg-easy-51.title: Type conversion

pg-easy-52.syntax:
-- General form: typed literal of a time span
INTERVAL 'quantity unit [quantity unit ...]' [fields]
'quantity unit'::interval

-- Examples
SELECT INTERVAL '3 hours 15 minutes';      -- 03:15:00
SELECT now() + INTERVAL '2 weeks';         -- timestamptz shifted by 14 days
SELECT '1 year 2 mons'::interval;          -- 1 year 2 mons
SELECT pg_typeof(INTERVAL '5 minutes');    -- interval

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- Stored as months, days, and microseconds separately, so
--   '1 month' <> '30 days' when added to dates, and
--   '1 day' <> '24 hours' across DST changes for timestamptz.
-- ISO 8601 form also works: INTERVAL 'P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S'
-- Field restriction: INTERVAL '90' MINUTE; INTERVAL '1-2' YEAR TO MONTH
-- extract(epoch FROM INTERVAL '2 hours') -> 7200 (seconds as numeric)
-- make_interval(days => 3, hours => 4) builds one from parts
-- date - date returns integer days, but timestamp - timestamp returns interval
-- justify_hours / justify_days normalize 36 hours -> 1 day 12:00:00
-- Output style is controlled by the IntervalStyle setting
pg-easy-52.title: Date/time types

pg-easy-53.syntax:
-- General form: timestamp +/- interval -> timestamp
SELECT <timestamp_expr> + INTERVAL '<quantity> <unit>';

-- Examples
SELECT current_timestamp - INTERVAL '3 hours';
SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-03-01 09:30' + INTERVAL '2 days 4 hours';
-- => 2024-03-03 13:30:00

-- now() = current_timestamp = transaction_timestamp():
--   fixed at the START of the current transaction, so it returns
--   the same value for every row and every call in that transaction.
-- clock_timestamp()      -> real wall-clock time, changes per call
-- statement_timestamp()  -> start of the current statement

-- Gotchas:
-- date + integer -> date        (CURRENT_DATE + 5)
-- date + interval -> timestamp  (time part becomes 00:00:00)
-- timestamptz + '1 day' respects DST (keeps wall-clock time);
--   '24 hours' adds exactly 24h.
-- Cast to drop the time: (now() + INTERVAL '1 month')::date
-- Month math clamps: DATE '2024-01-31' + INTERVAL '1 month'
--   => 2024-02-29 00:00:00
pg-easy-53.title: Date/time functions and operators

pg-easy-54.syntax:
-- General form: symbolic difference as an interval
AGE(later timestamp, earlier timestamp) -> interval
AGE(ts timestamp) -> interval  -- vs current_date (midnight)

-- Examples
SELECT age(timestamp '2020-06-15', timestamp '2018-03-10');
-- 2 years 3 mons 5 days  (years/months/days, not raw days)

SELECT age(timestamp '2019-03-01', timestamp '2019-02-01');
-- 1 mon  (not '28 days')

-- Gotchas:
-- * Result is calendar-aware: whole years/months first, then days.
-- * Argument order matters: age(earlier, later) gives a negative interval.
-- * Plain subtraction differs: timestamp - timestamp gives days/hours,
--   e.g. timestamp '2020-03-01' - timestamp '2019-03-01' = '366 days'.
-- * date - date returns an integer number of days.
-- * Extract parts with EXTRACT(YEAR FROM age(...)) or date_part('year', ...).
-- * justify_days()/justify_interval() normalize day-based intervals.
pg-easy-54.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-56.syntax:
-- General form
-- STRING_AGG(expression text, delimiter text [ORDER BY ...]) -> text
-- Concatenates non-null input values into one string, delimiter between them.

-- Example: one comma-separated list per group
SELECT dept, STRING_AGG(employee, '; ') AS staff
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept;

-- Example: control the order inside the aggregate
SELECT STRING_AGG(city, ' | ' ORDER BY city DESC) FROM offices;

-- Variations & gotchas:
-- * Order is NOT guaranteed unless you add ORDER BY inside the call.
-- * NULL values are skipped; if all inputs are NULL (or no rows), result is NULL.
--   Wrap with COALESCE(..., '') to get an empty string instead.
-- * Delimiter is not added before the first or after the last value.
-- * Non-text inputs need a cast: STRING_AGG(id::text, ',').
-- * DISTINCT works: STRING_AGG(DISTINCT color, ',' ORDER BY color).
-- * Also accepts bytea: STRING_AGG(bytes_col, '\x00'::bytea).
-- * Need an array instead? Use ARRAY_AGG(expr).
-- * The reverse (text -> rows) is STRING_TO_TABLE(text, delim) or
--   REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE.
pg-easy-56.title: Aggregate functions

pg-easy-58.syntax:
-- General form: POSIX regular expression match operators
-- string ~   pattern   -- matches, case-sensitive
-- string ~*  pattern   -- matches, case-insensitive
-- string !~  pattern   -- does NOT match, case-sensitive
-- string !~* pattern   -- does NOT match, case-insensitive

SELECT 'Postgres' ~  '^post';    -- false (case differs)
SELECT 'Postgres' ~* '^post';    -- true  (case ignored, anchored at start)
SELECT 'Postgres' ~* 'GRE';      -- true  (unanchored: matches anywhere)
SELECT 'Postgres' !~* '^sql';    -- true  (does not start with sql)

SELECT city FROM offices WHERE city ~* '^san ';

-- Gotchas:
-- Regex is unanchored by default; use ^ for start, $ for end.
-- LIKE/ILIKE must match the WHOLE string; ~ / ~* match any substring.
-- ILIKE 'abc%' is the LIKE equivalent of ~* '^abc'.
-- Escape metacharacters (. * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \) to match literally.
-- NULL ~ 'x' yields NULL, not false.
pg-easy-58.title: Pattern matching

pg-easy-60.syntax:
-- General form: NULL-safe comparison
-- expr IS DISTINCT FROM expr      -- like <>, but NULL-aware
-- expr IS NOT DISTINCT FROM expr  -- like =,  but NULL-aware

-- Ordinary comparison returns NULL if either side is NULL
SELECT 5 <> NULL;                          -- NULL (unknown)
SELECT NULL = NULL;                        -- NULL (unknown)

-- NULL-aware comparison always returns true or false
SELECT 5 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;            -- true
SELECT NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;         -- false
SELECT NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL;     -- true

-- Find rows whose value changed, including to or from NULL
SELECT id FROM orders o JOIN orders_audit h USING (id)
WHERE o.status IS DISTINCT FROM h.status;

-- Gotchas:
-- * WHERE x <> 'shipped' silently skips rows where x is NULL;
--   WHERE x IS DISTINCT FROM 'shipped' includes them.
-- * NULL is not treated as ''; '' IS DISTINCT FROM NULL is true.
-- * No error is raised on NULL input; the result is just never NULL.
-- * IS NOT DISTINCT FROM usually can't use a plain btree index the way
--   '=' can, so prefer '=' when columns are NOT NULL.
-- * For a single value use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead.
pg-easy-60.title: Comparison operators

docs.title: SQL commands reference: data import and export

pg-easy-65.syntax:
-- General form
COPY table_name [(col1, col2, ...)]
  FROM { 'server_file' | STDIN | PROGRAM 'cmd' }
  [WITH (FORMAT csv|text|binary, HEADER, DELIMITER ',', NULL '')];
COPY { table_name | (SELECT ...) } TO { 'file' | STDOUT };

-- Load a CSV into a table (one command, rows streamed in)
COPY products (sku, name, price)
  FROM '/srv/import/products.csv'
  WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);

-- Export query results
COPY (SELECT sku, price FROM products WHERE price > 50)
  TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);

-- psql client-side variant: reads a file on YOUR machine
-- \copy products FROM 'products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

-- Gotchas:
-- * Server-side files need superuser or pg_read_server_files /
--   pg_write_server_files; use \copy or STDIN otherwise.
-- * Parsed and planned once, not once per row.
-- * Constraints, triggers and index updates still happen per row.
-- * One bad row aborts the whole COPY by default
--   (PG 17+: ON_ERROR ignore for data type errors).
-- * For big loads: drop indexes/FKs first, recreate after;
--   raise maintenance_work_mem; run ANALYZE afterward.
-- * FREEZE option works only if the table was created or
--   truncated in the same transaction.
pg-easy-65.title: Data loading

pg-easy-74.syntax:
-- General form: $tag$ ... $tag$  (tag is optional, may be empty)
-- Text between the delimiters is taken literally: no escape processing,
-- single quotes and backslashes need no doubling.
SELECT $$O'Brien's book$$;          -- O'Brien's book
SELECT 'O''Brien''s book';          -- same value, standard quoting

-- Tagged form lets you nest dollar quotes (e.g. function bodies)
CREATE FUNCTION greet(name text) RETURNS text AS $fn$
  SELECT 'Hi, ' || name || $q$ -- it's $$ fine $$ here$q$;
$fn$ LANGUAGE sql;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Tags are case-sensitive: $Tag$ ... $tag$ do not match.
-- * Tag follows identifier rules, no $ inside it; $1 is a parameter, not a quote.
-- * No variable interpolation: $$x = $var$$ is just text.
-- * Backslashes are literal: $$a\nb$$ is 4 chars (a, \, n, b).
-- * Result type is unknown/text like any literal; no effect on collation
--   or case sensitivity of comparisons.
-- * Multi-line strings also work with ordinary '...' literals.
-- * A dollar-quote following an identifier char needs whitespace: x$$..$$ fails.
pg-easy-74.title: String literals and quoting

docs.title: Queries: table expressions and select lists

pg-easy-76.title: Query syntax

pg-easy-79.syntax:
-- General form: collect input values (including NULLs) into an array
array_agg(expression [ORDER BY sort_expr [ASC|DESC]])

-- One array per group
SELECT dept_id, array_agg(employee_name)
FROM staff
GROUP BY dept_id;
-- dept_id | array_agg
--       1 | {Ana,Ben,Ana}

-- Control element order inside the array
SELECT team, array_agg(score ORDER BY score DESC)
FROM results
GROUP BY team;

-- Variations & gotchas:
-- * Duplicates are kept; use array_agg(DISTINCT x) to drop them.
-- * NULL inputs become NULL elements; filter with
--   array_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL).
-- * Without ORDER BY, element order is unspecified.
-- * With no input rows, the result is NULL, not '{}';
--   use COALESCE(array_agg(x), '{}').
-- * Array inputs produce a multidimensional array (all must match size).
-- * For a delimited text string instead, use string_agg(x, ', ').
pg-easy-79.title: Aggregate functions

pg-easy-80.syntax:
-- General form (psql client only, not SQL; no trailing semicolon)
\! [ command ]

-- Runs an OS shell command and returns to the psql prompt
\! ls -l /var/backups
\! date

-- With no argument: starts an interactive subshell;
-- type 'exit' to come back to psql
\!

-- Example: check a file before importing it
\! head -n 3 /data/orders.csv
\copy orders FROM '/data/orders.csv' CSV HEADER

-- Gotchas:
-- * Runs on the CLIENT machine, not the database server
-- * The rest of the line is passed to the shell unchanged
--   (psql does not expand :variables or handle quoting)
-- * The shell comes from $SHELL (default /bin/sh); Windows uses cmd.exe
-- * Cannot be used inside a single-line \\ separated list reliably;
--   put it on its own line
-- Related: \cd dir changes the client working directory,
--   \setenv NAME value sets an env var for child processes,
--   \g | cmd pipes a query's output to a shell command
pg-easy-80.title: psql meta-commands

docs.title: System Administration Functions: Database Object Management

pg-easy-82.syntax:
-- General form
pg_size_pretty(bigint | numeric) -> text   -- e.g. '8192 bytes', '24 MB'
pg_total_relation_size(regclass) -> bigint  -- table + indexes + TOAST
pg_relation_size(regclass [, fork text]) -> bigint  -- main fork only by default
pg_table_size(regclass) -> bigint           -- table + TOAST, no indexes
pg_indexes_size(regclass) -> bigint         -- all indexes on the table

-- Examples
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('invoices'));
-- e.g. '156 MB' (text)

SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size(oid))   AS data,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(oid)) AS idx
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- Gotchas
-- pg_size_pretty returns text: sort by the raw bigint, not the
--   pretty string ('9 MB' > '10 GB' as text).
-- Units are powers of 1024 (kB, MB, GB, TB, PB).
-- pg_size_bytes('1.5 GB') converts back to bigint.
-- pg_database_size('mydb') sizes a whole database.
-- Sizes are on-disk bytes, not row counts; use
--   pg_class.reltuples for an estimated row count.
pg-easy-82.title: System administration functions

pg-easy-84.syntax:
-- General form
NULLIF(value1, value2)
-- Returns NULL if value1 = value2; otherwise returns value1.
-- Equivalent to: CASE WHEN value1 = value2 THEN NULL ELSE value1 END

-- Example: avoid division-by-zero errors
SELECT total_cost / NULLIF(units_sold, 0) AS unit_price
FROM sales;
-- units_sold = 0  -> divisor is NULL -> result is NULL (no error)

-- Example: treat empty strings as missing
SELECT NULLIF(trim(nickname), '') AS nickname FROM members;
-- '' -> NULL ; 'Sam' -> 'Sam'

-- Combine with COALESCE to supply a fallback
SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(region, 'n/a'), 'Unknown') FROM offices;

-- Gotchas:
-- * NULLIF(5, 7) returns 5 (first argument, unchanged).
-- * NULLIF(NULL, 3) returns NULL; NULLIF(4, NULL) returns 4
--   (comparison with NULL is never true).
-- * Arguments must be comparable types; result type is that of the first argument.
-- * Not the inverse of COALESCE: COALESCE replaces NULLs, NULLIF creates them.
pg-easy-84.title: Conditional expressions

pg-easy-88.syntax:
-- General form
EXTRACT(field FROM source)   -- source: date, timestamp, time, interval
-- Returns numeric (PG 14+; double precision before 14)

-- Examples
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR  FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 2023
SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 11 (a number, not 'November')
SELECT EXTRACT(DOW   FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 2 (Sunday = 0)
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM TIMESTAMP '2023-11-07 00:00'); -- seconds since 1970

-- Common fields: CENTURY, YEAR, QUARTER, MONTH, WEEK, DAY, DOW, ISODOW,
--   DOY, HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND, EPOCH
-- date_part('month', ts) is the older equivalent (returns double precision)

-- Gotchas:
-- * For a month NAME, use to_char(ship_date, 'Month') or 'Mon' -> text
--   ('Month' is blank-padded to 9 chars; use 'FMMonth' to trim)
-- * To round down to the 1st of the month, use date_trunc('month', ship_date)
-- * Months between dates: use age() and extract YEAR*12 + MONTH from it
-- * EXTRACT(MONTH FROM INTERVAL '14 months') -> 2 (the remainder, not 14)
-- * Grouping by month alone mixes years; group by YEAR and MONTH together
pg-easy-88.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-89.syntax:
-- General form
date_trunc(field, source [, time_zone])
-- field: 'microseconds','milliseconds','second','minute','hour',
--        'day','week','month','quarter','year','decade','century','millennium'
-- Truncates (rounds DOWN) to the start of that unit; smaller fields are zeroed.

SELECT date_trunc('hour', timestamp '2023-11-17 14:47:09');
-- 2023-11-17 14:00:00

SELECT date_trunc('year', timestamp '2023-11-17 14:47:09');
-- 2023-01-01 00:00:00

-- Group rows per week
SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS wk, count(*)
FROM signups GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Never rounds to nearest: '2023-11-29' -> 2023-11-01, not 12-01.
-- * A date input is cast to timestamp(tz), so the result is a timestamp,
--   not a date; add ::date if you want a date.
-- * 'week' truncates to Monday (ISO weeks).
-- * To get a part as a number use extract(month FROM ts) / date_part.
-- * For text like '2023-11' use to_char(ts, 'YYYY-MM').
-- * With timestamptz, truncation uses the session TimeZone unless
--   the third time_zone argument is given (PG 12+).
-- * date_bin(stride, ts, origin) (PG 14+) buckets into arbitrary intervals.
pg-easy-89.title: Date/time functions

pg-easy-91.syntax:
-- General form: backslash + d + object-type letter(s), optional modifiers and pattern
-- \d[S+] [pattern]   describe one relation, or list relations if no pattern
\dv                   -- list views in the search path
\dv+ sales.*          -- views in schema sales, with size/description
\dt inventory_*       -- ordinary tables matching a pattern
\di                   -- indexes
\dm                   -- materialized views
\ds                   -- sequences
\dE                   -- foreign tables
\d order_summary      -- describe a single view: columns plus its definition
\sv order_summary     -- show the view's CREATE statement

-- Letters combine: \dtv lists tables AND views together
-- S adds system objects:  \dvS  (includes pg_catalog/information_schema views)
-- + adds extra columns (size, description, persistence)
-- Patterns use * and ? wildcards; 'schema.name' qualifies by schema
-- Gotchas:
--   \dv does NOT include materialized views; use \dm for those
--   Without a pattern, only objects visible in search_path are listed
--   Meta-commands run in psql only, not as SQL from other clients
pg-easy-91.title: psql meta-commands

pg-easy-92.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S][+] [pattern]

-- Examples:
\du                -- list roles with their attributes and memberships
\du app_*          -- only roles whose names start with app_
\du+               -- adds the Description column
\dg                -- same output as \du (kept for 'groups')

-- Related listing commands:
--   \dt  tables       \dv  views       \dn  schemas
--   \di  indexes      \ds  sequences   \df  functions
--   \l   databases    \dp  access privileges

-- Gotchas:
--  * Meta-commands start with a backslash and need no semicolon.
--  * They only work in psql, not in other clients or drivers.
--  * Patterns are wildcards (* and ?), not LIKE syntax.
--  * Add S to include system objects, e.g. \dtS.
--  * The SQL equivalent for roles is:
--      SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles;
--  * PostgreSQL has only roles; 'users' and 'groups' are roles
--    with or without LOGIN.
pg-easy-92.title: psql meta-commands

pg-easy-95.syntax:
-- General form: subscripts are 1-based; slices use lower:upper (inclusive)
-- array_expr[n]          -> single element
-- array_expr[lo:hi]      -> sub-array from lo to hi, both inclusive

SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d','e'])[4];      -- 'd'
SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d','e'])[2:4];    -- {b,c,d}
SELECT (ARRAY[5,6,7,8,9])[:2];               -- {5,6}   (omitted lower = start)
SELECT (ARRAY[5,6,7,8,9])[4:];               -- {8,9}   (omitted upper = end)

-- Gotchas:
-- * Indexing starts at 1, not 0.
-- * A slice always returns an array, even [3:3] -> {7}; plain [3] returns a scalar.
-- * Out-of-range subscript returns NULL; out-of-range slice returns an empty array '{}'.
-- * A literal ARRAY[...] needs parentheses before subscripting: (ARRAY[...])[i].
-- * If any dimension is written as a slice, all dimensions are treated as slices;
--   for 2-D arrays, arr[1:2][2] means arr[1:2][1:2].
-- * Arrays display with braces, e.g. {6,7}, not square brackets.
-- * array_lower/array_upper/array_length(arr, 1) report the bounds.
pg-easy-95.title: Arrays

pg-easy-96.syntax:
-- General form: a LATERAL item may reference columns of FROM items listed before it
SELECT ...
FROM left_item alias,
     LATERAL (subquery using alias.col) sub_alias;

-- Explicit join form (same as comma for inner semantics)
SELECT ... FROM a CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...) s;

-- Example: latest 2 posts per author
SELECT au.username, p.title
FROM authors au
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT title FROM posts
  WHERE posts.author_id = au.author_id
  ORDER BY published_at DESC
  LIMIT 2
) p;

-- Keep outer rows with no match: LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true
SELECT d.dept_name, e.emp_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT emp_name FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.dept_id
  ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1
) e ON true;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Comma / CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops outer rows whose subquery returns nothing.
-- * The subquery is conceptually evaluated once per row of the preceding items.
-- * Only items to the LEFT can be referenced.
-- * Functions in FROM are implicitly lateral: FROM t, generate_series(1, t.n)
-- * Without LATERAL, referencing an earlier FROM item in a subquery is an error.
pg-easy-96.title: Subqueries in the FROM clause

docs.title: Lexical Structure: Identifiers and Key Words

pg-easy-97.syntax:
-- General form: wrap an identifier in double quotes
SELECT "column_name" FROM "table_name";

-- Reserved words must be quoted when used as identifiers
CREATE TABLE "user" (id int, "select" text);
SELECT "select" FROM "user" WHERE id = 1;

-- Schema-qualified: quote each part separately
SELECT * FROM public."group";

-- Gotchas:
-- 'text' in single quotes is a string literal, never an identifier
--   SELECT * FROM 'group';   -- syntax error
-- Unquoted names are folded to lower case:
--   MyTable = mytable, but "MyTable" is a different, case-sensitive name
-- Once created quoted with capitals, you must always quote it the same way
-- To include a double quote inside a name, write it twice: "a""b"
-- Non-reserved key words (e.g. name, value) may be used unquoted
-- quote_ident('group') returns the safely quoted form for dynamic SQL
-- Best practice: avoid reserved words as names to skip quoting entirely
pg-easy-97.title: Identifiers and key words

pg-easy-98.syntax:
-- General form: delay the CURRENT session's execution
pg_sleep(seconds double precision)        -- returns void
pg_sleep_for(interval)                    -- PG 9.4+
pg_sleep_until(timestamp with time zone)  -- PG 9.4+

-- Examples
SELECT pg_sleep(0.5);                     -- half a second (fractions allowed)
SELECT pg_sleep_for('3 minutes');
SELECT pg_sleep_until('tomorrow 03:00');

-- Only the calling backend sleeps; other sessions keep running.
-- Argument is in SECONDS, not milliseconds: pg_sleep(1.5) = 1.5 s.
-- Effective resolution is platform-specific; 0.01 s is common.
-- Locks already held are NOT released while sleeping, so sleeping
-- inside a transaction can block other sessions.
-- statement_timeout still applies and can cancel a long sleep.
-- Called once per row if used in a SELECT list over a table:
--   SELECT pg_sleep(0.1) FROM generate_series(1,5);  -- ~0.5 s total
-- Handy for testing timeouts, lock waits, and monitoring scripts.
pg-easy-98.title: Date/time functions and server utilities

pg-easy-99.syntax:
-- General form
random()                      -- double precision, 0.0 <= x < 1.0
random(min, max)              -- PG17+: integer/bigint/numeric, min <= x <= max (both inclusive)
random_normal(mean, stddev)   -- PG16+: normally distributed value
setseed(seed)                 -- seed between -1.0 and 1.0

-- Examples
SELECT floor(random() * 6)::int + 1 AS die_roll;   -- 1..6
SELECT random(10, 20);                             -- 10..20, PG17+
SELECT setseed(0.42); SELECT random();             -- repeatable sequence
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY random() LIMIT 3;  -- random sample (slow on big tables)

-- Gotchas
-- random() includes 0.0 but excludes 1.0 (half-open range)
-- floor(random() * n) gives 0..n-1; round() makes the end values half as likely
-- random() is VOLATILE: it is evaluated again for every row
-- setseed() affects only the current session
-- Not cryptographically secure; use pgcrypto gen_random_bytes() for secrets
-- For sampling large tables, consider TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM / BERNOULLI
pg-easy-99.title: Mathematical functions

pg-easy-100.syntax:
-- General form: a string constant is text enclosed in single quotes
'text here'

-- To include a single quote inside, write two adjacent single quotes
SELECT 'it''s here';            -- result: it's here
SELECT 'O''Brien''s pub';       -- result: O'Brien's pub
SELECT '''quoted''';            -- result: 'quoted'

-- Variations:
-- Escape string syntax (E prefix) also accepts backslash escapes
SELECT E'can\'t stop';          -- result: can't stop

-- Dollar quoting avoids doubling quotes entirely
SELECT $$won't need doubling$$;
SELECT $tag$a 'b' c$tag$;

-- Gotchas:
-- Double quotes (") delimit identifiers, not strings: "col" is a column name
-- Two literals separated only by whitespace that includes a newline are
--   concatenated: 'foo'
--   'bar' -> 'foobar' (but 'foo' 'bar' on one line is a syntax error)
-- With standard_conforming_strings = on (default), a backslash in '...'
--   is a literal backslash; use E'...' for backslash escapes
-- In application code, prefer bound parameters over manual quote escaping
pg-easy-100.title: String constants and literals

pg-easy-104.syntax:
-- A B-tree index can serve an anchored prefix match when the
-- column is compared directly, not wrapped in a function.
-- General form:
--   WHERE col LIKE 'prefix%'
-- The planner rewrites it to a range: col >= 'prefix' AND col < 'prefiy'

CREATE INDEX orders_code_idx ON orders (code COLLATE "C");

-- Uses the index (Index/Bitmap scan):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE code LIKE 'ORD-77%';

-- Same idea, written as an explicit range:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE code >= 'ORD-77' AND code < 'ORD-78';

-- Cannot use a plain index on code (function hides the column):
--   WHERE substr(code, 1, 6) = 'ORD-77'
--   WHERE lower(code) LIKE 'ord-77%'
-- Fix: index the expression itself:
CREATE INDEX orders_code_lower_idx ON orders (lower(code));

-- Gotchas:
-- * Non-C collations: a default B-tree index cannot serve LIKE.
--   Use an operator class instead:
--   CREATE INDEX ON orders (code text_pattern_ops);
-- * Leading wildcard ('%77') cannot use B-tree; consider pg_trgm.
-- * ILIKE uses the index only when the prefix has no letters.
-- * Check with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) to confirm the plan.
pg-easy-104.title: Indexes and query planning
